The story

The story of Seiko began in 1881 when Kintarō Hattori opened a watch and clock shop in Tokyo. In 1892, he established the 'Seikosha' factory to produce clocks, and later, in 1913, the company created Japan's first wristwatch, the Laurel. The first watch to bear the Seiko name on the dial was introduced in 1924. Key turning points for the brand include the launch of the Grand Seiko in 1960, which aimed to create the most accurate wristwatch possible, and its role as the official timekeeper for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics. A period of significant innovation followed, with the introduction of Japan's first diver's watch in 1965, a precursor to the Prospex line, and the release of the Seiko 5 Sports in 1968, which became popular for its durability and wide range of designs. In 1969, Seiko revolutionized the watch industry with the introduction of the Astron, the world's first quartz wristwatch. The company continued to innovate with the development of the Prospex Speedtimer, one of the world's first automatic chronographs, also in 1969, and later with technologies like the solar-powered watch in 1977 and the Kinetic movement in 1988. Today, Seiko remains a major force in the watchmaking world, producing a vast array of timepieces under various model lines. This includes the affordable and robust Seiko 5 Sports, the professional-grade Prospex series with models like the 'King Turtle', and the historically inspired Alpinist. The brand also revived the prestigious King Seiko line, once a high-end mechanical watch collection from the 1960s and 70s. Seiko continues to be known for its in-house manufacturing capabilities and its development of unique technologies like the Spring Drive movement, which combines mechanical and electronic elements.
